title: Newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE)
blurb: Explain the NIPE screen of eyes, heart, hips and testes, its timing (by 72 hours and at 6 to 8 weeks), hip risk factors and each screen-positive referral pathway.
question: Baby Ella was breech at the 36-week appointment, had a successful ECV and was born head first at 40 weeks. Her NIPE hip examination at 30 hours is normal. Does she need a hip ultrasound, and when?

teach.body: Formally: the NHS Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) screening programme aims to identify and refer babies born with congenital abnormalities of the eyes, heart, hips and (in males) testes, where detectable, within 72 hours of birth, and again at 6 to 8 weeks. In plain English: a full top-to-toe check, with four parts that are formal screens. It needs verbal parental consent, documented; parents can decline all or part.
teach.cite: NIPE screening programme handbook (updated Oct 2025); NICE NG194 1.3.3

items.label: Newborn examination
items.sub: KPI NP1; before discharge if born in hospital

items.label: Classed as delayed
items.sub: complete as soon as possible; record why

teach.caption: Babies born before 34+0 weeks with a hip referral: ultrasound at 38-40 weeks corrected age. Positive hip at the 6-8 week check: paediatric orthopaedics, seen by 10 weeks.

teach.h: The red reflex across skin tones
teach.body: The red reflex is the reflection of light from the back of the eye, seen as a red glow through the ophthalmoscope. It varies with ethnicity: orange-red in white babies, and it may appear less bright or magnolia in Black, Asian and minority ethnic babies. It is abnormal if it is completely or partially obscured, white, abnormally shaped, or asymmetrical between the eyes. Congenital cataract needs early surgery, usually at 6 to 10 weeks, which is why referral is fast.

items: Explain the screen and obtain verbal consent; document it.
Parents may decline all or part of the examination: make sure they understand each element and the possible consequences.
Record the decision and inform the GP and health visitor.
Record results and any referrals; tell parents what was found and what happens next.
If unsure of findings, ask for review by a senior neonatal clinician within 24 hours.

teach.body: Ella was breech at 36 weeks, so she has a NIPE national hip risk factor even though ECV worked and she was born head first. Her normal hip examination does not remove the risk factor. She was born at 40 weeks (34+0 or more), so she needs a hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age, with an outcome decision (discharge or orthopaedic assessment) by 6 weeks. The midwife explains this to her parents, records it, and makes sure the referral is made.
teach.cite: NIPE handbook 14.2, 14.11; newborn hip screen-positive pathway

teach.text: "She's head down now, so the breech doesn't count" is wrong. Breech at or after 36 completed weeks is a hip risk factor whatever the presentation at birth, including after successful ECV. Also, asymmetric skin creases are no longer a screen-positive hip finding.

items: NIPE screens eyes, heart, hips and testes: by 72 hours and at 6 to 8 weeks.
Abnormal red reflex: ophthalmologist within 2 weeks.
Hip risk factors: family history, breech at or after 36 weeks (even after ECV), breech at birth from 28 weeks.
Hip referral: ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks if born at 34+0 or more.
Any impalpable testis, or an undescended testis with hypospadias: consultant paediatrician within 24 hours.

summary: You can now explain the four parts of the NIPE screen, when the newborn and infant examinations happen, and how consent and declining work. You can identify hip risk factors and route each screen-positive finding to the right specialist on time.

A.q: By what age should the NIPE newborn screening examination be completed?
A.why: NIPE handbook and KPI NP1: the newborn screening examination should be completed before, or at, 72 hours of age. NG194 1.3.3 also requires an examination within 72 hours.

whyNot.0: There is no lower age limit, and 24 hours is not the standard; the deadline is 72 hours.
whyNot.1: Day 5 is when the blood spot sample is usually taken.
whyNot.3: After 72 hours the examination is classed as delayed.

A.q: Which four areas are the formal screening elements of the NIPE examination?
A.why: The NIPE programme screens for congenital abnormalities of the eyes, heart, hips and (in males) testes.

whyNot.1: Hearing is screened by the separate newborn hearing screening programme.
whyNot.2: Lungs and spine are checked in the full examination but are not NIPE screening elements.
whyNot.3: The palate is checked in the full examination but is not one of the four NIPE screens.

A.q: The midwife finds an abnormal red reflex in Baby Theo's left eye at the newborn examination. What is the referral standard?
A.why: NIPE eye screen-positive pathway: an ophthalmology specialist should provide clinical assessment by 2 weeks after screening.

whyNot.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays cataract treatment, usually done at 6 to 10 weeks.
whyNot.1: 24-hour consultant review is the pathway for urgent testes or heart findings; an abnormal red reflex goes to ophthalmology.
whyNot.2: An optometrist at 3 months is far too late and is not the NIPE pathway.

B.q: Which baby has a NIPE national hip risk factor?
options: A baby with asymmetric thigh skin creases
A baby whose sister needed a hip harness
A baby born at 37 weeks by caesarean
A baby whose aunt had a hip replacement
B.why: NIPE 14.2: a first-degree family history (parents or siblings) of a hip problem in early life needing splint, harness or operation is a national hip risk factor.

whyNot.0: Skin crease asymmetry is no longer a screen-positive finding in NIPE.
whyNot.2: Caesarean birth is not a risk factor; breech presentation is.
whyNot.3: An aunt is not a first-degree relative, and an adult hip replacement is not a hip problem in early life.

B.q: Baby Kai, born at 39 weeks, has a hip risk factor and a normal hip examination. When should his hip ultrasound be done?
B.why: NIPE hip pathway: for babies born at 34+0 weeks or more, perform hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age, so that an outcome decision is made by 6 weeks (NIPE 14.11).

whyNot.0: Hip ultrasound is not done in the first 24 hours.
whyNot.1: 2 weeks is the eye referral standard.
whyNot.2: The outcome decision should already have been made by 6 weeks, so the scan cannot wait for the infant check.

B.q: At the newborn examination, Baby Ravi has bilateral impalpable testes. What does the NIPE pathway require?
options: GP review at the 6-8 week check
Hip and renal ultrasound at 6 weeks
B.why: NIPE 15.10: bilateral impalpable testes need review by a consultant paediatrician or associate specialist within 24 hours, to rule out conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

whyNot.0: GP review at 6 to 8 weeks is for a palpable testis not in the scrotum without hypospadias.
whyNot.1: Ultrasound at 6 weeks is not the testes pathway and delays urgent review.

C.q: Twins Ada and Ben are born at 37 weeks. Ada was breech at birth; Ben was cephalic. Both have normal hip examinations. What should happen?
options: Hip ultrasound for both at 4-6 weeks
Hip ultrasound for Ada at 4-6 weeks
No ultrasound, as both examinations are normal
Ultrasound for Ada; Ben at the 6-8 week check
C.why: NIPE 14.3: all babies from a multiple pregnancy where any hip risk factor is present should have a hip ultrasound, because it can be hard to identify which baby was affected.

whyNot.1: In a multiple pregnancy all babies are referred when any risk factor is present.
whyNot.2: A risk factor needs ultrasound even when the examination is normal.
whyNot.3: Ben should also have an ultrasound, not wait for the infant check.

C.q: Mo and Sara decline the hip part of their baby's NIPE examination but accept the rest. What should the midwife do?
options: Insist the full examination is needed
Do the hip check while the baby sleeps
Inform, record, and tell the GP and HV
Refer the baby for hip ultrasound instead
C.why: NIPE: parents may decline all or part of the examination. Make sure they understand each element and the implications, record the decision, and inform the GP and health visitor.

whyNot.0: Parents have the right to decline all or part of screening.
whyNot.1: Examining without consent breaches their decision.
whyNot.3: Referral for ultrasound is a screening action they have not consented to.

C.q: Baby Noor, a Black baby, is examined at 40 hours. The midwife sees a less bright, magnolia-coloured red reflex that is equal in both eyes, with no shadows. What is the best interpretation?
options: Abnormal: refer to ophthalmology by 2 weeks
Unclear: repeat at the 6-8 week check
C.why: NIPE 12.8: the red reflex varies with ethnicity and can appear less bright and magnolia in Black, Asian and minority ethnic babies. Symmetrical with no shadows is a normal finding.

whyNot.0: Abnormal reflexes are obscured, white, misshapen or asymmetrical; this one is symmetrical with no shadows.
whyNot.2: There is no screen-positive finding needing urgent senior review.
whyNot.3: A clear, normal finding does not need deferring; she still has the routine infant check.

reteach.title: Eyes 2 weeks, testes 24 hours, hips 4 to 6 weeks
reteach.question: The NIPE referral times are easy to confuse. How can you anchor each one?

blocks.h: Match the urgency to the risk
blocks.body: Testes that cannot be felt at all on both sides could signal a disorder of sex development such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which can be life-threatening: consultant paediatrician within 24 hours (also for one impalpable testis, or an undescended testis with hypospadias). Cataract needs surgery at about 6 to 10 weeks: ophthalmologist by 2 weeks. Hips need time for ultrasound to be accurate: scan at 4 to 6 weeks, outcome decision by 6 weeks.

blocks.text: A normal hip examination does NOT cancel a risk factor. Breech at 36 weeks or later, breech at birth from 28 weeks, or a first-degree family history all mean ultrasound.

explain.body: Newborn examination by 72 hours (later = delayed; complete as soon as possible and record why). Infant examination at 6 to 8 weeks. Verbal consent documented; parents can decline all or part.

test.q: A NIPE newborn examination was missed and the baby is now 80 hours old. What should happen?
options: Skip it and do the 6-8 week check
Wait for the community midwife on day 10
Repeat the blood spot test instead
Complete it promptly and record why
test.why: NIPE handbook: an examination not completed by 72 hours is classed as delayed and should be completed as soon as possible by the current care provider, with the reason recorded.

whyNot.0: The newborn examination is not skipped; it is completed late.
whyNot.1: Waiting until day 10 adds unnecessary delay.
whyNot.2: The blood spot is a separate screen and does not replace NIPE.

explain.body: The red reflex is checked with an ophthalmoscope. Abnormal if obscured, white, misshapen or asymmetrical. Main target: congenital cataract. Referral: ophthalmologist by 2 weeks after screening.

test.q: What is the main condition the NIPE eye screen aims to detect?
test.why: NIPE handbook: the main aim of the eye screen is to identify congenital cataracts, which need early detection and treatment.

whyNot.0: Squint is not the primary target of the newborn eye screen.
whyNot.2: Conjunctivitis is an infection, not a screening target.
whyNot.3: Retinopathy of prematurity has its own screening for preterm babies.

explain.body: Observe colour, breathing and feeding; palpate femoral pulses (weak or absent may suggest coarctation); auscultate. Critical heart disease does not always cause a murmur. Pulse oximetry is not a universal screen. Screen positive: urgent escalation to a paediatric or neonatal consultant, with review within 24 hours.

test.q: During the NIPE heart screen, weak femoral pulses may suggest which condition?
test.why: NIPE handbook 13: absent or weak femoral pulses may suggest certain types of congenital heart disease, including coarctation of the aorta.

whyNot.1: An ASD does not typically weaken femoral pulses.
whyNot.2: A patent foramen ovale does not cause weak femoral pulses.
whyNot.3: An innocent murmur is not associated with weak femoral pulses.

explain.body: Hips: Barlow and Ortolani on each hip, plus risk factors; ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks (born at 34+0 or more). Testes: bilateral impalpable, impalpable with or without hypospadias, or palpable with hypospadias: consultant paediatrician within 24 hours; palpable testis not in scrotum without hypospadias: GP at 6 to 8 weeks.

test.q: Baby Luca has a right testis felt in the groin, not the scrotum, and no hypospadias. What is the NIPE pathway?
options: GP review at the 6-8 week check
Ultrasound of the groin at 4 weeks
test.why: NIPE 15.9-15.11: one or both testes palpable but not in the scrotum, without hypospadias, need non-urgent review by the GP at the 6 to 8 week infant examination.

whyNot.0: 24-hour review is for impalpable testes or findings with hypospadias.
whyNot.1: A 2-week urology referral is not the NIPE pathway.
whyNot.3: Groin ultrasound is not part of the NIPE testes pathway.
